passages: [prose] Recorded species were characterised following the functional classification of Kitahara and Fujii (1994, 1997). On the basis of resource utilisation patterns by species, these authors proposed a classification according to 2 fundamental niche dimensions (time and food). Applying the generalist/ specialist concept to the analysis of butterfly community structure, they classified butterfly species based on 2 representative traits: larval resource breadth (range of host-plant species used by larvae) and voltinism (number of generations per year). They considered host-plant specificity as an indicator of the niche breadth in a larval food dimension, while the notion of voltinism was extended to serve as a surrogate for the niche breadth in a seasonal time dimension (see Kitahara and Fujii 1994, 1997). This classification resulted in 4 functional groups: (i) typical specialists (TS) which are uni- or bivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 1 plant family only; (ii) typical generalists (TG) which are multivoltine species (3 generations or more per year) that feed on hostplants belonging to 2 or more plant families; (iii) rebound specialists (RS) which are multivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 1 plant family only; and selective generalists (SeG) which are uni- or bivoltine species that feed on host-plants belonging to 2 or more plant families (see Online Resource 1) (Santin 2004; Lafranchis 2000; Tolman and Lewington 1999).

[prose] Over the 2 years of the butterfly survey, 2459 individuals of 41 species were recorded within the 15 urban parks studied (see Online Resource 1 for species list). Among these 41 species, 12 TG species (1745 individuals), 5 RS species (268 individuals), 7 SeG species (289 individuals) and 17 TS species (157 individuals) were recorded.

[prose] As filtering of species in our study indicates that species vary in their dispersal opportunities, seasonal specificity as well as in feeding specialization, the mass-effect paradigm may apply to good dispersers able to cope with highly modified urban habitats (low disturbance susceptibility), but the species-sorting paradigm to those with low dispersal abilities and high habitat specificity (high disturbance susceptibility) (Leibold et al. 2004; Schleicher 2010). This assumption is consistent with the species composition found in adjacent natural areas, consisting in typical Mediterranean sclerophyllous forests and scrubs (Table 6). In these natural areas, dominant species are Mediterranean TS species, whereas TG species, dominating urban public parks, are represented by very few individuals. This may be due to the fact that metacommunity paradigms are not always distinct and especially mass-effect and species sorting models (Logue et al. 2011). With low dispersal, the mass-effect model indeed approaches a species sorting process (Driscoll 2008). In this study, we have focused our analysis on urban parks which constitute only a portion of a larger urbanization gradient. Dispersal limitation and environmental limitation (related to disturbance) seem to be preponderant in this urban portion, but the dominance of Mediterranean and/or specialist species in adjacent natural areas gives ground for considering an important role for interspecific competition and habitat filtering in less disturbed habitats according to the species sorting model (Leibold 1998).

As a first step, stepwise selections were performed, within each of the three groups of environmental variables, to exclude variables that did not contribute significantly to the explained variation in the 4 response variables (and thus to avoid saturated global model) . Thus, we performed a first series of (partial) regression analyses using redundancy analysis (RDA) and we selected variables within each group on the basis of Akaike information criterion (AIC) (Akaike 1978). We tested, for each environmental variable, both linear and quadratic terms. For each of the three sets of environmental variables (plot, park, landscape), the combination minimising the Akaike criterion was used to select the variables to include in the analysis. Note that for abundance of uni-bivoltine butterflies, analyses were performed on the 93 sampling plots where uni-bivoltine species occurred.

[prose] Moreover, this functional trait is also strongly correlated with a range of other ecological attributes (Barbaro and van Halder 2009; Laurance 1991). First, voltinism corresponds to reproductive parameters and breeding phenology (Barbaro and van Halder 2009), but is also associated with feeding habits. In our study, most of multivoltine species are polyphagous (of the 17 multivoltine species, 12 are polyphagous), while most of uni-bivoltine species are oligophagous (of the 24 uni-bivoltine species, 17 are oligophagous) (see Online Resource 1). Hence, multivoltine species can benefit from particular management practices in urban parks (such as flower planting and water supply), which favour the maintenance of exploitable resources during the period of summer drought that Bseasonal specialist^ species may not be able to exploit in one or two generations (Blair and Launer 1997; Graves and Shapiro 2003). Indeed, typical Mediterranean species, mostly uni-bivoltine, are often diapausing during this summer drought period. Thus, multivoltine butterflies could correspond to performing Burbanadapters^ (Blair and Launer 1997), especially under the Mediterranean climate, able to exploit urban resources better than Mediterranean species.

[prose] Then, to identify gradients of environmental variables that might influence the degree of nestedness, Spearman correlations between ranks of parks in both packed matrices on one hand, and between ranks of parks ordered according to species richness and environmental variables on the other hand, were calculated (Patterson and Atmar 2000). In the same way, Spearman correlation between the degree of rarity of species (species ranks in the packed matrix) and the degree of specialization of species was assessed (see Online Resource 1).

[prose] Habitat distribution did not show significantly nested patterns between parks (Table 4), except for matrix temperature (T) (Table 4), which is congruent with the matrix fill (72.5 %) as T is known to be sensitive to matrix fill (see Online Resource 4 for the packed matrix). However, ranks of parks between both packed matrices (according to species composition and habitat composition) were not significantly correlated (Spearman Rs=−0.30; p=0.28).

[prose] Spearman correlations between ranks of parks ordered according to nestedness in species composition highlighted that isolation of parks, composition of the surrounding landscape and fragmentation of vegetation units within parks determined nested structure in specific composition of parks (Table 5). This confirmed the importance of landscape features in structuring butterfly assemblages at plot level (as seen previously), but also at park level. [prose] Thus, taking into account the four theoretical metacommunity models, we can first exclude the neutral model (Hubbell 2001) because, in our study, species are filtered according to functional traits (cf. species ranks in the packed matrix – Online Resource 3) and are obviously not functionally equivalent. The patch-dynamics model (Levins and Culver 1971) can also be excluded as parks (differing in size, design and locality) cannot be considered constant in terms of habitat quality whereas patches are assumed to be identical in this theoretical model (Leibold et al. 2004). Therefore, if disturbance generates nested habitat patterns, this may lead to nested patterns in species composition predicted by the species sorting model (Leibold 1998) or the mass-effect model (Mouquet and Loreau 2003) of metacommunity. In effect, nested habitats can produce nested patterns in species assemblages under both these theoretical models (Driscoll 2008).
